title: (Re)searching for meaning
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, writing after ResearchED Ballarat, argues that educators must judge the quality of the evidence behind a practice and not merely whether something is labelled evidence-based. He notes that the phrase has become a marketing tool, and shows how easy it is to find a study supporting nearly any idea by tracing a learning-styles paper on virtual-reality underwater engineering and a UDL study whose conclusions do not match its own results. He explains why effect sizes can mislead, since they compare an intervention with no instruction, and why unrepresentative samples, as in wellbeing program research, can distort claims. He offers a rough hierarchy of peer-reviewed work, meta-analyses and personal cognitive bias, and recommends bodies like AERO that vet research for practitioners. The closing point is that schools too often adopt shiny programs on the strength of a single weak professional-learning session.
points: Evidence-based has become a sales label, so the useful question is about the quality, sampling and independence of the evidence behind a program.
Brien demonstrates the problem by quickly finding a flawed learning-styles study whose conclusions contradict its own results.
Education effect sizes are measured against no instruction, which makes even weak interventions like EdTech look positive.
Unrepresentative or undisclosed samples can curate a marketable evidence base for wellbeing programs.
He urges leaders to rely on vetted syntheses and be wary of their own confirmation bias.
quotes: No one is claiming that the Science of Learning or Explicit Teaching will solve everything in education, however it is our current ‘best bet’. We focus on the best of what we currently know.

Every professional development you attend refers to how evidence-based it is, becoming more of a marketing tool to sell their product than it is a gauge of the effectiveness. Much like how fitness influencers have successfully sold ice baths and tummy tea4 to the Instagram masses despite no evidence supporting their effectiveness (and some pointing towards potential harm).

Well first, the sample size of only 26 engineering students make it difficult to generalize to wider populations. Next, Kolb’s learning styles has long been debunked by cognitive science as a neuromyth.

For example EdTech has an effect size of 0.27 (while the hinge point of a positive impact is said to be 0.40) which means that yes, EdTech leads to learning happening when you compare it to a student being alone in a room with literally nothing. Crazy right? A teacher could probably do a mime performance about the new knowledge and it would still have a slightly positive effect size.

These programs can work in schools if they are implemented well, however the evidence base behind them is carefully curated to create a perfectly marketable product. It also provides a straw-man when these programs do not work in a school that it must be the schools poor implementation and not the appropriateness of the program itself for their cohort.

The greatest issue that come alongside there being research that exists to support any educational hypothesis is that teachers will be able to find evidence to support any of their internal beliefs. This can mean that bad ideas can become psychologically sticky as the sound good, look good but in reality are all style and no substance.

Too often do schools or leaders within schools launch into a shiny new set of strategies or programs because a single shady professional learning session ran by someone who has not been in a classroom since the 1990s has managed to swindle them into implementing. Our students deserve more than that. Our staff deserve more than that.
